title: Constitutional Amendment 2: School Elections and Partisan Elections

context.text: Referred to voters by the New Mexico Legislature as a proposed constitutional amendment; the Secretary of State lists it among four amendments on the November 3, 2026 ballot. A majority of the votes cast on the question is needed to adopt it.

question.text: Proposing to amend Article 7, Section 1 of the Constitution of New Mexico to remove the requirement that school elections be separate from partisan elections.

summary.text: Removes the constitutional provision that all school elections be held at different times from partisan elections. School districts could then place bond and mill levy questions on the even-year general election ballot, and the legislature could by law allow school board elections to be held with partisan elections; the amendment does not require either. The guide says a special all-mail school election can cost $125,000 to $250,000 depending on district size and number of issues.

measure.yesMeans: Removes the requirement that school elections be held separately from partisan elections.
measure.noMeans: Keeps the requirement that school elections be held at different times from partisan elections.

argumentsFor.text: Voter guide argument for: "School districts will save the cost of expensive all-mail ballots."
Voter guide argument for: "More participation in school elections." It says participation rates for statewide general elections tend to be much higher than for local elections.

argumentsAgainst.text: Voter guide argument against: "Adding school questions to the general election ballot could create voter fatigue and increased costs."
Voter guide argument against: "The amendment may lead to politicizing school district elections." It notes voters approved the separation requirement in 2008.

researchNotes: Source: the New Mexico Secretary of State's 2026 Voter Guide and its published ballot question text. The guide reproduces purpose statements and arguments for and against prepared by the legislature (it links nmlegis.gov's Constitutional Amendments 2026 publication) and states that this analysis does not necessarily reflect the Secretary of State's views; arguments are the guide's unattributed summaries, not statements by named campaigns. The Secretary of State says only the title (in capital letters on the joint resolution) appears on the ballot. Required vote: a simple majority. Legislative vote tallies were not retrieved.
